title: Typing Functions
objective: After this lesson you will be able to type function parameters, returns, optional/default/rest parameters and callbacks, distinguish void from never, and read overload signatures in library code.
why: Functions are where types earn their keep: almost every runtime bug crosses a function boundary. A function's signature is a contract — takes these, returns that — and a typed signature is executable documentation that the compiler enforces at every call site, forever, across every file that touches it.

blocks.text: The full signature
You've been typing parameters since Lesson 1. The complete picture adds the return type after the parameter list:

The return annotation is worth writing on any shared function for two reasons: it documents the contract for callers, and it catches accidental drift — if a refactor starts returning `null` where a `string` was promised, the compiler flags the *function*, not a distant consumer.
Optional, default and rest parameters
Parameters have three modifiers that map directly to how you already design APIs:

items: Optional (`?`) parameters become `T | undefined` inside the function — you must handle the missing case.
Default parameters get their type *from* the default value; annotate only if the default is narrower than what you accept.
Rest parameters collect everything remaining into a typed array — the last parameter only.

blocks.title: Common mistake #4
blocks.text: Placing an optional parameter before a required one: `function f(a?: string, b: number)`. TypeScript rejects it (required can't follow optional). If you genuinely want a leading optional, use `a?: string | undefined` explicitly — or reorder, which is almost always the better API.
void: "I don't return anything"

`void` says the return value should be ignored. It's the return type of side-effect functions like `log`. The subtlety worth knowing: a `void`-returning type also accepts functions that *do* return something — because the caller is declaring it won't use the result:
never: "this cannot happen"

`never` is the type of code that doesn't finish: a function that always throws, or an infinite loop. It's not `void` (which finishes, returning nothing). `never` shines in exhaustiveness checking — the pattern you'll use constantly with Lesson 5's unions:

blocks.title: Why the never trick matters
blocks.text: When a teammate adds `"success"` to the state union later, the default branch stops compiling — TypeScript points at the exact switch statement you forgot to update. It converts future refactoring mistakes into present compile errors.
Function types: callbacks as parameters
Functions are values, so they have types. Spell them with arrow syntax — the most common typed-callback patterns:

Notice how `applyAll`'s callback needs **no annotations at the call site** — the generic parameters (Lesson 6 deep-dives) flow the element type into the callback's parameter automatically. That's inference working across function boundaries, and it's why typed code isn't more verbose than JavaScript.
Overloads: one name, multiple contracts

Sometimes a function legitimately behaves differently per input shape. Overload signatures declare each contract; the implementation must satisfy them all. You'll *read* overloads in every major library, so learn to recognize the shape:

Callers only see the overload signatures — the implementation signature is invisible from outside. In modern TypeScript, unions + narrowing (Lesson 5) cover many cases overloads used to handle; prefer the simpler union when the body logic is shared, and reserve overloads for genuinely different contracts.
How it appears in real applications
A retry wrapper — the kind of utility every codebase grows — types cleanly with everything from this lesson:

Default `attempts`, an optional observer callback typed as `(error: unknown, attempt: number) => void`, a generic `T` tying input promise to output promise, and an error held as `unknown` — every idea from the last three lessons cooperating in one function.

items: Full signatures are (params): ReturnType; annotate returns on shared functions to lock contracts
Optional (?), default and rest parameters map 1:1 to API design intent; defaults infer their type
void = caller ignores the result; never = code that cannot finish — the exhaustiveness-checking workhorse
Callback types use arrow syntax; generics flow element types into callbacks so call sites stay clean
Overloads declare multiple visible contracts over one implementation — prefer unions when the logic is shared

exercise.prompt: Write a typed `pipe` utility: pipe(f, g) returns a function that runs f, passes its result to g, and returns g's result — with types so precise that pipe(toString, double) fails to compile but pipe(double, toString) works, where `const double = (n: number) => n * 2` and `const toString = (n: number) => `n=${n}``... wait — that's the two-argument version. Keep it to two functions and make the output of the first feed the input of the second, enforced by the compiler.
hints: Start from the types of the two functions you'll accept: what must be true about f's output and g's input?
Name it: `function pipe<A, B>(f: (a: A) => B, g: (b: B) => ???)` — the second function's input is the first's output type.
The result is a function you can call later: the return type of pipe is itself a function type — (a: A) => D where g: (b: B) => D.
exercise.why: The chain B — f produces it, g consumes it — is exactly what generics encode. The compiler literally checks the arrows connect: f's output type flows into g's parameter slot. When pipe(show, double) is attempted, B is string but g wants number, and the mismatch is a compile error instead of a NaN at runtime. This same shape underlies every compose/pipe utility in real codebases (and fp-ts, RxJS map chains, etc.).

quiz.q: function notify(user: string, message?: string): void — which call is invalid?
options: notify("ada")
notify("ada", "hello")
notify("ada", undefined)
notify(undefined, "hello")
quiz.explain: The first parameter is required (string, not optional). Passing undefined there is an error. The message parameter accepts a string or can be omitted entirely — passing undefined explicitly is also allowed for optional parameters.

options: Nothing — they're synonyms
void = returns but value ignored; never = execution never completes (throws or loops forever)
never = returns undefined; void = returns null
never is only for async functions
quiz.explain: A void function completes; its return value is just ignored by contract. A never function never returns control at all — the compiler tracks this, which is why code after `fail(...)` is treated as unreachable and exhaustiveness checks work.

quiz.q: type Handler = (e: {type: string}) => void — const h: Handler = (e) => e.type.length works. Why does e need no annotation?
options: Arrow functions can't be annotated
Contextual typing: the assignment target's type flows into the parameter automatically
e is implicitly any, which is allowed here
void callbacks skip parameter checking
quiz.explain: Contextual typing is inference across function boundaries: when a function expression is assigned to a typed target, its parameters adopt the target's parameter types. This is why callbacks in typed APIs stay annotation-free.

quiz.q: Inside `if (value === undefined) fail(...); return value;` — why does the return compile when value was `T | undefined`?
options: strict mode is off in that file
fail's never return type tells control-flow analysis that reaching the return means undefined was eliminated
The compiler doesn't check returns after if-statements
undefined is assignable to T
quiz.explain: TypeScript's control-flow analysis removes impossible states per branch. If the undefined path throws (never), the only way to reach `return value` is with value defined — so the type has narrowed to T.

quiz.q: You see two bare signatures above a concrete implementation in library code. What are they?
options: Dead code the library forgot to remove
Overload declarations — the visible contracts callers match against; the third is the hidden implementation
Deprecated syntax from TypeScript 1.x
JSDoc hints the compiler ignores
quiz.explain: That two-signatures-then-implementation stack is the overload pattern: callers see only the declared overloads. Recognizing it turns intimidating library type definitions into readable contracts.

summary: Function signatures are contracts enforced at every call site: parameters take the modifiers you design APIs with (? for optional, defaults that infer, rest as arrays), return types lock behavior against drift, void and never say "ignore the result" and "cannot finish" respectively, and callback arrow types + contextual typing keep higher-order code as terse as JavaScript. Overloads declare multi-contract functions when unions can't.
next: So far every value has had exactly one type. Lesson 5 introduces unions — values that are honestly one of several things — and the narrowing machinery that makes unions a superpower instead of a liability.
